title: Projection engine is one 1,700-line closure-heavy function behind a wildcard-import facade

evidence.description: src/projection_stages/deterministic_engine.py:91-1792 — run_deterministic_projection_stage — it is the only top-level def in the file and spans about 1,700 lines. It holds 20+ nested helpers (_next_housing_for_year 152, _next_housing_sale_inputs 231, _medicare_month_fraction 421, _wellness_premium_for_age 446, _ss_first_claim_year_month_fraction 488, _inflate_brackets_path 516 ...), and none of them can be imported or unit-tested on their own.

evidence.symbol: module header / engine_kernels re-export / from .core import * / rmd_divisor rebinding / project docstring
evidence.description: src/planning_engines.py:177-183 — `from .core import *` then `rmd_divisor = _rmd_divisor_with_table_override` — shows that the wildcard import has already shadowed a function with a narrower signature (Wave 5 N5) and needed a manual rebinding. Lines 49-163 re-export about 110 kernel names (including the typing names Callable, Dict, Iterable) so that callers and monkeypatch targets keep working. Lines 193-199 keep code text in a docstring as 'migration breadcrumbs for legacy source-inspection regression tests'. The file is 3,050 lines.
src/engine_kernels.py:19 — wildcard import of core — a second 2,415-line engine module pulls in the whole of core's namespace.
src/reporting/workbook_common.py:16 — wildcard import — the reporting layer also takes all of core, and workbook_builder.py (comments at 595/662/835) relies on `from .workbook_common import *`.

observed_behavior: The year-by-year engine already has 26 extracted stage modules, but the orchestration and many domain calculations (housing steps, mortgage amortization, Medicare month fractions, survivor factors, bracket inflation) still live as closures inside one function. The facade modules use wildcard imports with no __all__ on core and keep a large re-export list so that older call sites and monkeypatch targets keep working.
impact: These are the files that change in every engine fix (PRs #419 and #420 touched this area). The closures cannot be tested in isolation, so they are checked only through whole-projection golden masters, which makes each change risky and slow to verify. Wildcard imports have already caused one silent signature-shadowing defect and can cause another the next time core gains a name.
root_cause: 8 engine files were consolidated into one to avoid circular imports (planning_engines.py:3-14), and stage extraction stopped at the stage boundary without lifting the shared per-year helpers.
options: Replace the remaining wildcard imports (engine_kernels.py:19, planning_engines.py:177, workbook_common.py:16) with explicit name lists, using the AST method already applied in deterministic_engine.py:46-52, and give core an explicit __all__. Low effort; removes the shadowing class of defect.

Lift the nested helpers of run_deterministic_projection_stage into pure functions in projection_stages modules with explicit inputs, one group per change, each verified by golden-master equality. Medium-to-high effort, incremental.
Leave the structure and rely on golden masters. No effort, but the defect class and the review cost both remain.
recommendation: Do option 1 first because it is cheap and mechanical. Then do option 2 incrementally, starting with the housing and Medicare helpers, which are the most self-contained. Narrow the planning_engines re-export list once callers import from engine_kernels directly.
dependencies: Golden-master and phase-golden baselines must be stable before each extraction
implementation_considerations: Tests that monkeypatch facade names (for example tests/test_lcv_feasibility_gate_regression.py:103,116 patch planning_engines.LCV_FEASIBILITY_GATE_THRESHOLD) depend on where a name is bound. Moving a name changes which binding a patch affects. Remove the docstring breadcrumbs together with the source-inspection tests that need them.
risk_of_change: Medium. These are pure refactors of financial-critical code, so any accidental behaviour change shows up only as golden-master drift.
verification_method: Run golden-master and phase-golden equality before and after each step with no regeneration. A static check that no `import *` remains in src/.
verification_rationale: I opened src/projection_stages/deterministic_engine.py. Line 91 is the only top-level def, run_deterministic_projection_stage, and the file is 1,792 lines. It contains 37 nested defs at 4-space indent (for example _mortgage_payment_and_balance 125, _next_housing_for_year 152, _next_housing_sale_inputs 231), so the count of '20+ helpers' is an understatement. src/planning_engines.py:177-183 confirms the `from .core import *` and the rmd_divisor rebinding comment (W5-2/N5) that explicitly names the shadowing defect. The docstring breadcrumbs are at 193-199. src/engine_kernels.py:19 and src/reporting/workbook_common.py:16 confirm the wildcard imports. grep finds no __all__ in src/core.py. Mitigation already in place: deterministic_engine.py:46-52 uses an explicit AST-derived import list, which shows option 1 is workable. Medium severity holds: this is maintainability risk with one real past defect, not a current wrong output. I did not open the planning_engines re-export list at 49-163 line by line.

title: Layer inversion: housing domain and engine import pricing logic from the server-services layer, and src imports the separate Trends reporter

evidence.description: src/server_services/strategy_asset_service.py:218-260 — estimate_housing_cost — the docstring calls it the 'pure pricing core'. It holds hard-coded city and population multipliers and STATE_ESTIMATES defaults inside a 1,256-line service module whose layer is described as request-independent business logic.
src/housing_comparison.py:53-57 — an engine-level domain module imports from the service layer.

src/housing/api.py:23, src/housing/optimizer.py:24, src/housing/plan_variant.py:14, src/housing/results.py:10, src/housing/zip_screen/screen.py:14 — five housing-domain modules import constants or functions from server_services.strategy_asset_service (git grep output).
src/housing/plan_variant.py:72-78 — _years_out — its docstring says it re-implements the 'same formula estimate_housing_cost uses internally', which is duplicated logic caused by the misplaced owner.

documentation/reference/SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE_DIAGRAM.md:39-50 — the generated import graph shows `Core Engine & Domain --> Server Services` and `--> HTTP Routes` edges. Lines 68-78 list `financial_trends_reporter` as an undeclared 'third-party' import of the HTTP Routes layer.

src/server/workbook_routes.py:626 — `from financial_trends_reporter.live_snapshot import classify_symbol` — the main app depends on the separately launched reporter package for asset-class classification. Meanwhile, ten reporter modules import from src (for example financial_trends_reporter/live_snapshot.py:134-1266 and financial_trends_reporter/main.py:30-45), so the two packages depend on each other.

observed_behavior: Housing pricing rules and constants live in a service module and are imported downward by the housing domain package and by housing_comparison. The main app's holdings route imports the classifier that the Trends reporter owns, while the reporter imports widely from src.
impact: A change to the service layer can change engine and housing-optimizer results. The housing formula is already duplicated (plan_variant._years_out) because its owner sits in the wrong layer. The bidirectional src/reporter coupling means neither package can be versioned, packaged or tested alone, and a reporter refactor can break the main app's /api/holdings/classes route.
root_cause: Pricing was extracted from an HTTP payload function into the nearest module (strategy_asset_service, H8 slice 3) rather than into the housing domain package. classify_symbol was written for the reporter first and reused in place.
options: Move estimate_housing_cost, STATE_ESTIMATES and the HOME_APPR/INFLATION defaults into a domain module (for example src/housing/pricing.py) and have strategy_asset_service import it. Move classify_symbol into src/portfolio_analytics.py and have the reporter import it from src. Add an import-direction rule (domain must not import server_services/server) to the diagram generator or fast gates.
Move the code only and do not add an enforcement rule. Cheaper, but the inversion can return.
Keep the current layout and document the exceptions in the module catalog.
recommendation: Take option 1. The moves are mechanical. The import-direction rule turns the generated diagram's bidirectional edges into a check rather than just an observation.
dependencies: Regenerate SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE_DIAGRAM.md as required by project rules
implementation_considerations: Keep re-exports in strategy_asset_service for one release if external tools import the names. Python tests that read panel JS as text are not affected.
risk_of_change: Low. These are pure moves with no formula change. Housing goldens should stay identical.
verification_method: Run housing and golden-master tests unchanged. The regenerated diagram should show no Core->Server Services or Core->HTTP Routes edges apart from the desktop_api adapter.
verification_rationale: git grep confirms that src/housing/{api,optimizer,plan_variant,results,zip_screen/screen}.py and src/housing_comparison.py:53 import from server_services.strategy_asset_service. src/housing/plan_variant.py:72-78 _years_out says in its docstring that it duplicates estimate_housing_cost's internal formula. src/server/workbook_routes.py:626 imports financial_trends_reporter.live_snapshot.classify_symbol inside get_holding_classes, and 17 tracked files in financial_trends_reporter import from src, so the dependency runs both ways. Because the import is lazy and inside a function, a reporter break would fail only that route, not app startup. That limits the impact somewhat but does not refute the finding. I did not open SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE_DIAGRAM.md lines 39-78, so that evidence item is unverified by me. The core claim stands on the import evidence alone.

title: Several modules log outside the 'retirement_system' logger tree, so their warnings never reach app.log or its redaction filters; startup migration failures are dropped on the desktop path

evidence.description: src/bootstrap.py:81-104 — configure_logging — the only file handler (rotating local_state/logs/app.log, with _RedactingFormatter and MaskingFilter) is attached to the 'retirement_system' logger only. No root handler is configured anywhere: a git grep for basicConfig or root handlers in src, main.py, financial_trends_reporter and tools/launchers found nothing.

src/sales_tax_year.py:25,170 — the logger is 'src.sales_tax_year', outside the configured tree. Its record 'wash detection failed; the loss is shown whole' (a tax-relevant degradation) and the automatic wash-scan failure (342) bypass app.log.
src/year_end.py:184 — the year-end safe-default fallback is logged to 'src.year_end', which has no handler.
src/data_io.py:328 — 'unparseable number ...; using default' goes to 'src.data_io', which has no handler.
src/market_data.py:298 — 'Stored API keys unavailable' is logged via getLogger(__name__), which has no handler.
src/fallback_log.py:14 and src/report_compute.py:31 use 'retirement_system.*' names correctly, which shows the convention exists but is not applied consistently.
src/plan_data_migration.py:502-503 — the outer `except Exception: return {... 'skipped': True}` has no log call.
tools/launchers/START_DESKTOP.py:28 and src/desktop_api.py:49 discard the migration result. Only main.py:140-146 prints the error, and only to the console, never to app.log.
frontend/js/dashboard_decomp_local_backups.js:133 — `catch (_e) {}` — a failed automatic backup after save or build is silently ignored.

observed_behavior: Records from __name__-named loggers fall through to Python's lastResort handler, so WARNING and above go to stderr only (a console window in the frozen exe, retirement_planner.spec:142, with no file, no rotation and no redaction or account-number masking). Plan-data migration failures on the desktop-shortcut launch path are not recorded anywhere.
impact: When a user reports a wrong number, app.log does not contain the fallback that caused it (wash-sale detection skipped, year-end default used, unparseable plan value defaulted). stderr output also bypasses the MaskingFilter the project relies on to protect account numbers. Startup migration failures on the most common launch path are invisible, so the retry-every-boot design can fail forever without notice.
root_cause: The file handler is scoped to a named logger tree, but modules created later used the `getLogger(__name__)` idiom. Nothing checks that logger names fall under the tree.
options: Rename the four __name__ loggers to 'retirement_system.<module>' and add a fast-gate grep forbidding getLogger(__name__) in src/. Log the migration result (and errors) through the 'retirement_system' logger inside run_startup_bootstrap.
Attach the rotating handler and its filters to the root logger instead, so every library and module record is captured. Simpler, but third-party library noise lands in app.log.
Keep the setup and document that only 'retirement_system.*' records are persisted.
recommendation: Take option 1, and log migration errors in bootstrap so every launch path records them. Have the frontend backup catch call showMessage on failure, as runLocalBackupNow already does.
implementation_considerations: Keep MaskingFilter and _RedactingFormatter on the handler. If option 2 is chosen, check that the filters also apply to the extra records.
risk_of_change: Low. Only logging wiring changes.
verification_method: Unit-test that a record emitted from src.sales_tax_year's logger reaches a handler attached via configure_logging, and that run_startup_bootstrap logs an injected migration error.
verification_rationale: src/bootstrap.py configure_logging attaches the rotating handler, _RedactingFormatter and MaskingFilter only to logging.getLogger('retirement_system'). git grep for basicConfig and getLogger() across src, main.py, financial_trends_reporter and tools/launchers returns nothing, so no root handler exists. src/sales_tax_year.py:25, src/year_end.py:18, src/data_io.py:69 and src/market_data.py:298 use getLogger(__name__), giving 'src.*' names outside the tree. I confirmed their call sites: sales_tax_year 170 ('wash detection failed; the loss is shown whole') and 342, year_end 184, data_io 328. Without a handler these reach Python's lastResort handler and go to stderr at WARNING and above. retirement_planner.spec:142 sets console=True. run_startup_plan_data_migration (plan_data_migration.py:502-503) swallows exceptions with no log call. run_startup_bootstrap (bootstrap.py:110-140) returns the result without logging it, and START_DESKTOP.py:28 discards it. frontend/js/dashboard_decomp_local_backups.js:133 has an empty catch. Observability is degraded, but the migration's own fallback is designed to keep reads correct, so medium severity is appropriate. The claim that the masking bypass matters is plausible but unproven: I did not confirm that any of these messages carry account numbers.

title: Plan-file backups can silently miss committed data, and forward-only schema upgrades run on open with no pre-upgrade copy

evidence.description: src/local_backup_scheduler.py:151-160 — checkpoint_sqlite — runs `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(FULL)` without reading its (busy, log, checkpointed) result row and swallows every exception. An incomplete checkpoint is therefore indistinguishable from a complete one.

src/local_backup_scheduler.py:324-339 — run_backup — calls checkpoint_sqlite, then shutil.copy2 of the main database file only (no -wal file, no SQLite backup API), then records a sha256 manifest of the copy as the backup.
src/local_backup_scheduler.py:29 — `enabled: bool = False` — automatic backups are opt-in.

src/plan_db_replace.py:133-142 — _backup_with_api — the codebase already has a consistent-snapshot helper based on sqlite3 backup() and uses it when replacing the active plan, but the scheduler does not reuse it.
src/stores/db.py:94-123 — migrate — upgrades are forward-only ('There is no downgrade'). A newer file raises SchemaVersionError on older code.
src/stores/_base.py:113 — every writable open migrates the file in place. No copy is taken before the upgrade.

src/stores/plan_store.py:164-165 — 24 migrations. Some move data: src/stores/broker_repo.py:59-60,82-83 use INSERT...SELECT followed by DROP TABLE. plan_paths (222-245) derives a per-plan local_state/plan_backups/<id> folder but has no caller in src (git grep finds only re-exports in src/stores/__init__.py), so the designed per-plan backup location is unused.
frontend/js/dashboard_decomp_row_model.js:5455,5664 — automatic backups fire right after a save or build, when other connections are most likely to be active on the plan file.

observed_behavior: When the WAL checkpoint cannot finish, for example because another connection (a build or the Trends reporter process reading the active plan) is mid-read, the scheduled backup copies a main file that lacks recently committed transactions. Its manifest still reports success. Separately, opening a plan file on new code upgrades it in place with no copy, so reverting to the previous build means the file can no longer be opened.
impact: A user who restores from an automatic backup may silently lose recent edits. A user hit by a faulty migration, or who rolls back the app, has no automatic way back unless they had opted into backups. This is a data-integrity risk on the household's only copy of plan data, which matters for a non-expert user who will not know to make manual copies.
root_cause: Two backup implementations grew separately. The upgrade path was designed for atomic steps, not for reversibility.
options: Use the SQLite backup API (reuse plan_db_replace._backup_with_api) in run_backup, and check the checkpoint result. When _check_and_migrate finds version < current on a real file, write a one-time copy (for example into plan_paths(...).backups_dir) before migrating.
Only switch run_backup to the backup API and leave upgrades as they are. This fixes the silent-incomplete-backup risk only.
Enable daily backups by default instead. More coverage, but the copy method stays unsafe.
recommendation: Take option 1. Both parts are small, and they reuse code and a folder layout that already exist.
dependencies: ARC-003 (so that backup or pre-upgrade copy failures are logged)
implementation_considerations: The pre-upgrade copy must not run for :memory: stores or read-only opens, and it needs a retention cap. The backup API holds a read transaction, so a long build write can delay it, but it never produces a torn copy.
risk_of_change: Low to medium. The change touches the open path of every store.
verification_method: Unit test: hold an open write transaction or a reader on a WAL database, run run_backup, and assert that the backup contains every committed row. Unit test: open a v23 fixture and assert that a pre-upgrade copy exists at v23.
verification_rationale: Code facts confirmed. src/local_backup_scheduler.py:151-160 checkpoint_sqlite ignores the wal_checkpoint(FULL) result row and swallows all exceptions. run_backup (309-350) then copies only the main file with shutil.copy2 and records a sha256 manifest. BackupPolicy.enabled defaults to False (27). src/plan_db_replace.py:133-142 _backup_with_api uses sqlite3 backup() and is not reused. src/stores/db.py:1-8 states 'There is no downgrade', and stores/db.py:46 sets WAL mode. src/stores/_base.py:94-113 migrates in place on every writable open with no copy, and read-only opens refuse older versions. broker_repo.py:59-60,82-83 use INSERT...SELECT plus DROP TABLE. plan_paths has no caller in src apart from re-exports and docstring references. Reason for the downgrade to partial: the data-loss trigger is conditional and was not demonstrated. Python's sqlite3.connect sets a default 5-second busy timeout, so FULL waits for contending readers or writers before it gives up. Backups are opt-in, which shrinks exposure. The per-migration transaction (db.py) also means a failed migration step leaves the file at the last good version, which softens the 'faulty migration' half. The rollback/no-pre-upgrade-copy half is fully confirmed.

title: The frontend 'ratchet' line ceiling is raised during feature work and the decomposed modules are becoming new monoliths

evidence.description: tests/test_frontend_size_ratchet.py:8-18 — the docstring says 'The ceiling only ever moves DOWN ... the only supported way to change it'. Line 695 sets TOTAL_JS_MAX_LINES = 43_777.

Local git history of that line shows the ceiling going up in feature commits: 42,502 (e77c2975, 2026-11-03) -> 42,531 -> 42,570 -> 42,576 -> 42,579 -> 42,609 -> 43,298 (61a9d7f2, #388) -> 43,620 (425fd97a, nav redesign) -> 43,401 -> 43,752 -> 43,762 -> 43,818 (0bbfb472) -> 43,813 -> 43,777 (2c293e62, after removing 237 blank lines). That is a net rise of about 1,275 lines in one week.

wc -l: dashboard_decomp_row_model.js is 5,974 lines (the project CLAUDE.md table says 5,188), dashboard_decomp_housing_optimizer.js is 2,832 (table says 1,984) and dashboard.js is 6,474. Total frontend/js is 43,763 lines.

frontend/js/dashboard_decomp_local_backups.js:136-147 — cross-module calls still go through bare globals (for example maybeRunLocalBackup called from row_model), so the 'decomp' files are coupled through a shared global namespace.

observed_behavior: The guard meant to force extraction is treated as a budget that each feature PR raises (PR #390 states it raised the ceiling from 43,298 to 43,620). The growth has moved into the 'decomp' files that were created to shrink dashboard.js.
impact: Feature work in the main UI keeps landing in very large files coupled through globals. This raises regression risk, slows review, and reduces the value of the usability work the system relies on. The agent guidance table in CLAUDE.md, used to scope reads, is now stale by 800-850 lines on two files.
affected_workflows: Sales Ledger, Holdings, Year-End and nav features
root_cause: The ratchet caps only the total plus dashboard.js. It has no per-file cap on the decomp modules, and the rule against raising it is enforced only by convention.
options: Add per-file ceilings for the decomp modules over about 1,500 lines and require a recorded reason line next to any ceiling increase, so a raise is a visible decision.
Plan a focused extraction of dashboard_decomp_row_model.js (for example by feature area) and lower the ceilings afterwards.
Accept the growth and rename the guard a budget, so the docstring matches practice.
recommendation: Take options 1 and 2 together: per-file caps stop the shift of growth into the decomp files, and one scoped extraction pays down the current excess. Update the CLAUDE.md large-file table at the same time.
dependencies: Usability findings that add UI will compete for the same line budget
implementation_considerations: Python tests that read panel JS as text constrain where code can move (see project CLAUDE.md). Check those before extracting.
risk_of_change: Medium for the extraction (UI regressions). Low for the guard change.
verification_method: Static: per-file wc -l against the new ceilings. Run the existing frontend Node tests and Playwright e2e locally after the extraction.
verification_rationale: tests/test_frontend_size_ratchet.py:1-18 docstring says 'This is a ratchet, not a budget. The ceiling only ever moves DOWN'. Line 186 is DASHBOARD_JS_MAX_LINES = 6_477 and line 695 is TOTAL_JS_MAX_LINES = 43_777. These are the only two MAX_LINES constants, so there is no per-file cap on the decomp modules. `git log -L695,695` confirms rises in feature commits: 42,502 (e77c2975) up to 43,298 (61a9d7f2, #388), 43,620 (425fd97a), 43,818 (0bbfb472), and back down to 43,777 (2c293e62). The history before that also shows rises from 41,7xx. wc -l gives row_model 5,974, housing_optimizer 2,832, dashboard.js 6,474, and a frontend/js total of 43,763, which matches the finding and shows the CLAUDE.md table is stale. local_backups.js:136-147 confirms the bare-global bridge. I did not open the PR #390 text.

title: Version surfaces disagree (12 / v11 / 10.0.0) and the surface checker cannot see the stale banners

evidence.description: src/version.py:5 — VERSION = '12' — declared as the 'single source of truth'.
main.py:97 — hard-coded 'RETIREMENT PLAN SYSTEM v11  [server mode]'. src/server/__main__.py:16 hard-codes the same 'v11' banner.
pyproject.toml:56 and package.json:3 both say '10.0.0'. retirement_planner.spec:2 says 'v11'.

tools/check_version_surfaces.py:37 — the STALE patterns cover v8-era tokens and 'Retirement System v<old>'. Nothing matches the uppercase 'RETIREMENT PLAN SYSTEM v11' or the package manifests, so the drift is not detected.
frontend/admin.html:3,7 — the asset cache-buster is the fixed string '?v=v11-pricing-symbol-tester-msg-fix-1', so it does not change when the version changes.
tools/bump_version.py:6-12 — the bump updates version.py, index.html and admin.html text but not pyproject.toml, package.json, the server banners or the admin cache-buster.

observed_behavior: Server-mode users see 'v11' while the app reports v12 elsewhere. Package metadata says 10.0.0. The admin page's cache-busting tag never changes between releases.
impact: Users and support see conflicting versions. In server mode a browser may keep a cached admin.js after an upgrade. The impact is low but recurring, and the bump tool gives false confidence.
root_cause: Strings were hard-coded outside version.py, and the checker's patterns target older formats.
options: Derive the banners from src.version.release_label(), make the cache-buster use VERSION (or a build hash), and add pyproject/package.json to bump_version.py and the checker.
Drop the version from pyproject/package.json (set it to a placeholder) and fix only the banners.
recommendation: Take option 1. Each change is a one-line edit.
implementation_considerations: pyproject's version may be read by packaging tools, so keep it in sync rather than deleting it.
risk_of_change: Low.
verification_method: Extend check_version_surfaces with a case-insensitive 'SYSTEM v\d+' pattern and a manifest-version comparison, then run it statically.
verification_rationale: src/version.py:5 is VERSION='12'. main.py:97 and src/server/__main__.py:16 hard-code 'RETIREMENT PLAN SYSTEM v11'. pyproject.toml:56 and package.json:3 say 10.0.0, and retirement_planner.spec:2 says v11. tools/check_version_surfaces.py scans only src, frontend and tools: main.py at the repo root is not scanned. Its dynamic patterns (82-107) are 'Retirement System v', 'RetirementPlanSystem/' and '', which are case-sensitive and do not match 'RETIREMENT PLAN SYSTEM v11' in src/server/__main__.py. frontend/admin.html:3,7 uses the fixed cache-buster '?v=v11-pricing-symbol-tester-msg-fix-1'. The bump_version.py docstring lists no pyproject or package.json step. The impact is cosmetic or cache-related, so low severity is correct.

title: Compatibility layers kept with no exit criteria: the Results Explorer re-parses the XLSX on every index call, and parse-time shims survive the at-rest migration

evidence.description: src/detailed_results.py:944-968 — even when the semantic model exists, every index request reopens retirement_plan.xlsx (load_workbook at 822) to append 'Excel-only legacy pages ... until all pages have been migrated'. The result is not cached, unlike the result model (923-940). workbook_detailed_results (990-996) returns an index-shaped payload when a model exists, despite its docstring 'Return all result pages'.
src/detailed_results.py:861,897 — chart-dashboard sheets and the full mode load the entire workbook with read_only=False, the slowest openpyxl mode.

src/plan_data_migration.py:2-9 — the at-rest migration exists 'so the read paths can assume the current schema and drop the shims'. Yet src/data_io.py:628 and src/domain_models.py:193 still call migrate_sectioned_data on every parse, and data_io.py:821-829 still uses wife_/h_ internal keys.

src/legacy_conversion/__init__.py:1-2 — 'the one removable module ... WP11.6 deletes it'. It is still 2,993 lines across 17 files and still wired through src/server_services/conversion_service.py:49-50.
src/market_data.py:38 — a fallback USER_AGENT 'RetirementPlanSystem/8.4' for an ImportError on src.version, which cannot happen inside the package.

observed_behavior: Several migration-era dual paths are still in place without a recorded condition for removal. One of them adds an uncached workbook parse to every Results Explorer navigation.
impact: Results Explorer navigation pays an XLSX open per index request (cost not measured in this static review). Readers of the engine must understand both the old and the current plan shapes, and about 3k lines of conversion code remain to maintain.
root_cause: Migrations were completed in stages, and the shims were never given removal triggers.
options: Record an exit criterion for each shim (for example: semantic model covers all sheets, then delete the Excel fallback; plan_data schema stamped everywhere, then drop the parse-time migrate_sectioned_data call), and cache the Excel index keyed on the workbook mtime meanwhile.
Only cache the Excel index (a quick performance win) and leave the shims.
Leave everything as it is.
recommendation: Take option 1: cache now, and add the removal criteria to the module catalog or backlog so the shims eventually go away.
implementation_considerations: Keep legacy_conversion until there is evidence that no pre-v12 installs remain. The frontend distinguishes fallback sheets via source === 'excel_parser_fallback' (frontend/js/dashboard.js:2409, frontend/js/reports_ui.js:74).
risk_of_change: Low for caching. Medium for removing the shims.
verification_method: Measure Results Explorer index latency before and after caching on a real workbook. Run Golden masters to confirm that removing a parse shim changes no output.
verification_rationale: src/detailed_results.py:944-968 _merge_model_index_with_excel calls _excel_workbook_detailed_index on every index request, with no cache, while _RESULT_MODEL_CACHE (923-940) caches only the model. workbook_detailed_results (990-996) returns the merged index despite its docstring 'Return all result pages'. title: The QBI (Section 199A) deduction is a flat 20% of business income with none of the statutory limits
rule_year: 2018-present (made permanent by P.L. 119-21; the threshold phase-in range widens from 2026)
assumptions: How large the effect is depends on whether the household's taxable income during working years is above the 199A threshold (about $394,600 MFJ for 2025) and whether the business is a specified service trade or business (SSTB). Neither is known from the code. Rule type: hard-coded (rate 0.20 is a literal; no threshold, SSTB or wage inputs exist). Authority: statute (authoritative); the implementation is unverified.

evidence.description: qbi_ded = qbi_base * 0.20 with qbi_base = net_se - half_se_ded - sehi_ded; there is no taxable-income cap, threshold or SSTB test
qbi_ded = max(0, (distribution - sehi_ded) * 0.20); there is no 50%-of-W-2-wages limit even though the S-corp salary is known in the same block
The only later change to qbi_ded is the sole-proprietor 401(k) reduction
ded += qbi_ded and then taxable_inc = max(0, agi - ded), with no cap of 20% of (taxable income before QBI minus net capital gain)
qbi_eligible defaults TRUE. It is the only QBI input, so there is no field for SSTB status, W-2 wages or UBIA

observed_behavior: Whenever qbi_eligible is on, the engine deducts 20% of the QBI base in every working year, whatever the income level. Grep found no SSTB, threshold, W-2-wage or taxable-income limit anywhere in src/, and no limitation notice discloses this.
impact: Above the threshold, an SSTB owner's deduction phases to zero. The engine still deducts 20%, so with $300k of QBI it understates federal tax by about $21k a year at 35%. For a non-SSTB S-corp paying a $100k salary, the 50%-of-wages limit caps the deduction at $50k instead of $60k, about $3.5k a year. Below the threshold, the missing taxable-income cap matters only in years when deductions are large relative to income. Lifetime tax, net worth, the Roth sizing headroom and Monte Carlo replays all inherit the error. The commit message for PR #419 cites a real plan year with $640k of taxable income, so this household may be above the threshold. That income was not shown to come from business years.
affected_workflows: Roth conversion sizing during working years
Lifetime tax and terminal net worth
root_cause: QBI was modeled as a simple 20% rate on the base, and the statutory limitation layers were never added or disclosed.
options: No credible alternative; this is a correctness defect.
recommendation: Add two inputs: SSTB yes/no and, for the S-corp, the W-2 wages (already known as scorp_salary). Apply the threshold and phase-in (dated rows in tax_law_v10.json), the SSTB phase-out, the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of UBIA, and the overall cap of 20% of (taxable income before QBI minus net capital gain). Until that is built, show a limitation notice when qbi_eligible is on. A CPA should confirm the rule values and the household's SSTB status.
implementation_considerations: The overall cap needs taxable income before QBI, which exists only after deductions in apply_agi_and_tax. Apply the cap there, not in income.py. The deduction stacks with the standard/itemized choice (ded = max(std, item) + qbi), so it should stay outside that max.
risk_of_change: Moderate. Engine output changes in every working year for qbi_eligible plans, and goldens must be re-pinned after one delta is checked by hand.
verification_method: Add closed-form unit cases: below the threshold; an SSTB inside and above the phase-in range; a non-SSTB S-corp where the wage limit binds; a low-income year where the taxable-income cap binds. Check one year of the real plan by hand against Form 8995-A.
verification_rationale: Opened src/projection_stages/income.py:249-251 and 282-284. Both branches use a literal qbi_base*0.20. Lines 370-371 only apply the sole-prop 401(k) reduction. roth_conversion_and_agi_tax.py:883-886 adds qbi_ded after max(std, item) with no cap tied to taxable income. client_sections.py:477 defaults qbi_eligible to TRUE. Further evidence I found: client_sections.py:1295 parses c['scorp_qbi_phaseout'] (qbi_phaseout_applies), and grep shows nothing in src/ reads it. So the input exists and is ignored, which strengthens the finding. Also, sheets_strategy.py:162 describes the S-corp QBI as '20% of W-2 wages + allocable basis', which contradicts what the engine does. Jurisdiction (IRC 199A) and rule years are stated. The impact figures depend on the household's income and SSTB status, which are unknown. Medium severity is kept because the error grows with income and the household may be above the threshold.

title: The OBBBA senior deduction phase-out is applied once to the couple's combined $12,000, not to each spouse's $6,000
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC 151(d)(5)(C) as added by P.L. 119-21 sec. 70103)
assumptions: This reviewer reads the statute as reducing each qualifying person's $6,000 amount by 6% of MAGI above $150k (MFJ), so a couple who both qualify loses the whole deduction at $250k MAGI. The reviewer also recalls that Form 1040 Schedule 1-A computes it per person. No primary source was fetched in this run, so a CPA should confirm. Rule type: hard-coded literals (6_000, 150_000/75_000, 0.06). Authority: statute; the implementation is unverified.

evidence.description: base = 6_000 * n_over_65 and phaseout = 0.06 * (magi - threshold), then the code returns max(0, base - phaseout). The reduction comes off the combined amount once, so an MFJ couple who both qualify keeps part of the deduction up to $350k MAGI
n65 counts living members aged 65 or over, and the result is added to both the standard and the itemized deduction
The same function feeds the Roth sizer's deduction estimate
The existing tests check only MAGI = 0 cases. Grep found no test of the phase-out range for two qualifying spouses

observed_behavior: For an MFJ couple who are both 65 or over, the deduction is 12,000 - 0.06 x (MAGI - 150,000). At $250k MAGI the engine allows $6,000, while the per-person reading gives $0. The gap is largest at $250k ($6,000) and closes at $350k.
impact: Federal tax is understated by up to about $1,300-$1,450 a year (at 22-24%) for 2025-2028 when the couple's MAGI is between $150k and $350k. Roth-conversion years for retirees often fall in that band, so the Roth sizer's headroom and the optimizer's scores move too. It is bounded to four years.
root_cause: The phase-out was written against the aggregate deduction instead of each qualifying person's amount.
options: No credible alternative; this is a correctness defect.
recommendation: Once a CPA confirms the per-person reading, compute the deduction as sum over qualifying people of max(0, 6,000 - 0.06 x max(0, MAGI - threshold)). Add tests at $200k, $250k and $300k MAGI with two qualifiers.
dependencies: CPA confirmation of the statutory reading
implementation_considerations: The fix is one function, and both the AGI stage and the Roth estimate call it. A QSS year passes filing='MFJ', but QSS is not a joint return, so its threshold should arguably be $75k. Settle that in the same change.
risk_of_change: Low code risk. Golden values move for 2025-2028 years of 65+ couples.
verification_method: Unit cases against a hand-filled Schedule 1-A; then run tools/regen_golden_master.py measure and check one delta by hand.
verification_rationale: src/core.py:863-882 confirms base = 6000*n_over_65 and a single 6% reduction taken off the combined amount. Both apply_agi_and_tax (lines 862-864) and the Roth estimate (engine_kernels.py:2283-2284) call it. The only direct test calls in tests/ use MAGI 0.0 (test_survivor_deduction_alive_gating_regression.py:100-102, test_fill_to_bracket_deduction_headroom_regression.py:69,92), so no test covers the phase-out range. The per-person reading (each $6,000 reduced, full phase-out at $250k MFJ) matches my understanding of P.L. 119-21 sec. 70103 and IRS guidance. I did not open a primary source, so confidence stays medium. I lowered severity to low because the gap is at most about $6k of deduction (about $1.3-1.4k of tax), only in 2025-2028, and only for couples in the $150k-$350k MAGI band. The QSS-threshold note is a fair side observation.

title: The SALT deduction's state income tax is AGI x the flat state rate, so it counts income the state does not tax
jurisdiction: US federal itemized deduction (IRC 164) interacting with state income tax (Illinois and the other modeled states)
assumptions: The effect appears only when the household itemizes, or when the inflated SALT figure is what tips it into itemizing. Rule type: approximation hard-coded in the stage. Authority: unverified.

evidence.description: il_tax_est = agi * rate (0.0495 fallback), salt_gross = il_tax_est + prop_tax_yr, salt = min(salt_gross, salt_cap(...))
The engine's actual state tax leaves out retirement distributions, Roth conversions and Social Security when exempt_retirement and exempt_ss are set, and it uses graduated brackets for CA and NY
Illinois has exempt_retirement=TRUE and exempt_ss=TRUE, so IRA withdrawals, RMDs and conversions are not taxed by Illinois
item_ded = salt + char + mortgage interest + medical + senior bonus, and ded = max(std_ded, item_ded)

observed_behavior: The SALT component uses a state tax of AGI x rate. It is not the state tax the engine computes a few lines later. For an Illinois retiree with $300k of AGI that is mostly conversions and RMDs, the estimate is $14,850, while the modeled Illinois tax on the remaining investment income is about $1k.
impact: For itemizers, SALT can be overstated by roughly $10k-$15k in Illinois conversion and RMD years (capped by the $40,400 2026 cap), which understates federal tax by about $2.4k-$3.6k a year at 24%. The inflated figure can also flip a household from the standard deduction to itemizing. The Roth optimizer sees the same understated tax. Graduated states (CA/NY) get a flat-rate figure instead of their brackets.
affected_workflows: Roth conversion years in states that exempt retirement income
root_cause: State tax is computed after the deduction step, so the SALT step uses a flat proxy and does not call state_income_tax.
options: No credible alternative; this is a correctness defect.
recommendation: Feed SALT from state_income_tax (or a prior-year actual, matching cash-basis deduction timing) using the same income classification the state-tax call uses. Keep the cap logic unchanged.
implementation_considerations: state_income_tax needs earned_net and the retirement and SS classification, and all of them are known before line 764. Computing the state tax once and reusing it removes the circularity. The DAF makeup and HSA correction sub-stages recompute item_ded and must reuse the same SALT.
risk_of_change: Moderate. Itemizing households in states with retirement exemptions see federal tax rise. Re-pin goldens.
verification_method: A closed-form test of an Illinois household with a large conversion and high property tax: compare salt_gross with the computed state_tax plus property tax. Then measure the deltas and check one year by hand.
verification_rationale: roth_conversion_and_agi_tax.py:761-777 computes il_tax_est = agi * rate and feeds it into salt_gross. core.py:1052-1109 state_income_tax leaves out retirement_dist+roth_conv and SS when exempt flags are set, and it uses brackets for graduated states. state_tax.csv row 2 confirms Illinois exempt_retirement=TRUE and exempt_ss=TRUE. The SALT proxy therefore counts income Illinois does not tax. One mitigation limits the impact: when the property tax alone already reaches the SALT cap, the overstatement has no effect, so households with large Illinois property tax may see no change. The effect is otherwise real for itemizers and households near the itemizing threshold. Medium is kept.

title: Illinois estate tax runs the old state-death-tax-credit table on the whole estate, with no federal-tax limit and no $60,000 adjustment
jurisdiction: Illinois (35 ILCS 405/2(b), referencing IRC 2011 as in effect Dec 31, 2001)
assumptions: This reviewer understands Illinois tax as the IRC 2011(b) credit on the adjusted taxable estate (taxable estate less $60,000), limited to the federal tax computed with a $4M exclusion amount, with the interrelated deduction of the Illinois tax itself. That limit produces a steep phase-in above $4M, not a cliff. No primary source or Illinois Attorney General calculator was consulted in this run. Rule type: hard-coded table and method in code. Authority: secondary/unverified. An estate attorney must review.

evidence.description: This is the 2011(b) table keyed directly on the value passed in. No $60,000 is subtracted to get the adjusted taxable estate
Once the estate is over the exemption, the code solves T = credit(gross - T) with no limit at the federal tax over a $4M exclusion. The docstring calls it a cliff
Illinois tax on state_taxable feeds terminal estate tax and Post-Tax Inheritance
The Roth optimizer's estate penalty uses the same state calculation

observed_behavior: For a $4.1M Illinois taxable estate, the iteration converges to about $269k of tax. A calculation limited by the federal tax with a $4M exclusion would be on the order of 40% of the $100k excess before the interrelated deduction, about $40k. Above about $5M the credit table becomes the binding limit again, and the code then overstates by only the $60k adjustment (about $6.7k-$9.6k).
impact: For Illinois estates between about $4M and $5M, terminal estate tax and Post-Tax Inheritance may be overstated by up to roughly $230k. That also inflates the estate-penalty term the Roth optimizer and the CST-funding logic respond to. Lifetime spending results are not affected.
root_cause: The credit was implemented without the 2011(e)-style limit, which Illinois carries by reference, and without the adjusted-taxable-estate definition.
options: No credible alternative; this is a correctness defect.
recommendation: Have an estate attorney confirm the Illinois method, or compare against the Illinois Attorney General estate tax calculator. Then implement: adjusted taxable estate = TE - 60,000; credit = min(table(adjusted TE), tentative federal tax on TE with a $4M exclusion amount); and solve the interrelated deduction. Add calculator-matched test points at $4.05M, $4.5M, $5M and $10M.
implementation_considerations: The limit needs a section 2001 rate schedule, which the code does not have today (federal estate tax is a flat 40%). The NY branch is independent.
risk_of_change: Low code risk. Estate figures move for Illinois households above $4M.
verification_method: Compare against the Illinois Attorney General calculator at several estate sizes, with an attorney's sign-off.
verification_rationale: The code behavior is confirmed. core.py:1298-1318 applies the 2011(b) table to the raw value, and that table's 40,000 floor is the adjusted-taxable-estate table, yet no $60,000 is subtracted. core.py:1321-1338 solves T = credit(gross - T) with no limit tied to federal tax and calls the result a 'cliff' in its docstring. I recomputed credit(~3.83M) at about $269k, which matches the finding. after_tax.py:729-783 and roth_conversion.py:110-141 both feed the state calculation. The legal claim is that Illinois limits the credit to federal tax computed with a $4M exclusion, which would produce a phase-in rather than a cliff. I did not verify that against the statute or the Illinois AG calculator, and the finding admits the same. The missing $60k adjustment is the most likely error. The size of the overstatement in the $4M-$5M band depends on the unverified limit. This stays requires_external_domain_verification. Severity stays medium if the limit is confirmed; confidence is low.

title: In-force life insurance is report-only: death benefits never reach the survivor and are left out of the estate-tax base, without telling the user
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC 101(a), 2042) and state estate tax
assumptions: Applies when the Existing Life Insurance module is on and policies are entered. Policies owned by an ILIT are correctly outside the estate; others are not. Rule type: not modeled. Authority: statute.

evidence.description: The protection sheets 'do not feed the projection engine'
Face amount, insured, beneficiary and owned_by_ilit are parsed into c['life_policies']
The sheet shows inventory and coverage versus need only. No text tells the user the projection leaves the policies out
The estate base is total_nw plus business value. Life-insurance face is not added

observed_behavior: Grep found life_policies consumed only by the protection sheet and the module catalog. A death in the deterministic or Monte Carlo projection pays no death benefit into the survivor's accounts, and policies not owned by an ILIT are not included in the gross estate.
impact: Survivor scenarios understate the survivor's assets by the face amount (conservative). Estate tax is understated where an in-force non-ILIT policy pays at the measured death, which matters most against Illinois's $4M exclusion. A user who enters policies can reasonably assume they are part of the survivor analysis.
root_cause: The protection modules were delivered as Phase 1 report-only builders, and the projection was never integrated.
options: Option A: integrate. Pay the face amount (term in force at the death year) tax-free into the survivor's or beneficiary's taxable or cash account in the death year, stop premiums after the death or term end, and add non-ILIT face to the estate base. This is most accurate but changes engine output.
Option B: disclose. Add a limitation notice and a sheet banner saying policies are inventory-only and not in survivor or estate results. Low effort, but results stay incomplete.
Option C: do B now and A later behind a module switch.
recommendation: Option C. Ship the disclosure now, then integrate behind the existing module switch, with planner review of the beneficiary routing.
dependencies: Beneficiary and owner fields already parsed
implementation_considerations: Death years differ per Monte Carlo path (sample_death_year), so the benefit has to be applied per path, not replayed from the deterministic rows.
risk_of_change: Option B low; Option A moderate (survivor and estate outputs change).
verification_method: Scenario test: a $1M term policy on member 1 with a death in the projection. The survivor's balance should rise by $1M in the death year, and the estate base should include the face for a non-ILIT policy.
verification_rationale: sheets_protection.py:1-14 says the sheets 'do not feed the projection engine'. advanced_modules.py parses face_amount and owned_by_ilit. Grep shows life_policies used only in data_io defaults, module_catalog.py:918, advanced_modules and sheets_protection. No engine stage reads it, and I found no death-benefit payout for life policies anywhere outside reporting. after_tax.py:746-783 builds the estate base from total_nw plus business value only. The catalog entry (module_catalog.py:913-926) states no limitation. Leaving the benefit out of survivor assets is a conservative error. Leaving it out of the estate base is not. Whether users assume the policies are integrated is inferred, so confidence is lowered to medium. Medium severity is kept because estate tax against Illinois's $4M exclusion can move materially.

title: The self-employed health insurance deduction is counted again as itemized medical and is not reduced by the ACA premium credit
assumptions: The double count matters only when the household itemizes and medical costs exceed 7.5% of AGI. The credit issue matters only when earned income and a marketplace credit occur in the same year. Rule type: not modeled. Authority: statute.

evidence.description: The SEHI source is the gross bridge premium plus Part B/D/G, with no reduction for the premium credit
sehi_ded = min(source, net_se), or the S-corp version, is taken above the line
medical_expense_yr = wellness_premium_yr + ..., which includes the same premiums, and sehi_ded is not subtracted
The bridge premium is netted by the credit for cash, but the SEHI source still uses the gross premium

observed_behavior: Premiums already deducted under 162(l) are counted again as 213 medical expenses, and the SEHI deduction can exceed the premium the household actually pays after the credit.
impact: In the years it applies, taxable income is understated by up to the premium amount. The usual size is small to moderate, a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of tax a year.
affected_workflows: ACA bridge years with business income
root_cause: The SEHI and medical deductions are computed from the same premium figures without the statutory exclusion between them.
options: No credible alternative; this is a correctness defect.
recommendation: Subtract sehi_ded from the premium part of medical_expense_yr. Cap the SEHI source at premiums net of the credit, using the simplified iterative method in Rev. Proc. 2014-41.
implementation_considerations: The SEHI and credit interaction is circular. One or two fixed-point passes in the existing ACA recompute block are enough.
risk_of_change: Low.
verification_method: Unit test: an itemizing self-employed household with premiums. Medical deduction should exclude the premiums already deducted as SEHI. With a credit present, SEHI should be no more than the net premium.

That gross figure is not net of the PTC, while roth_conversion_and_agi_tax.py:698-707 does net the bridge premium by aca_ptc_yr for wellness_premium_yr. The double count matters only when the household itemizes and medical costs exceed 7.5% of AGI. Low severity is appropriate.

title: After the first death, the deceased spouse's unused federal estate exemption (DSUE) keeps growing with inflation
rule_year: Current law (P.L. 119-21 base $15M per person, indexed after 2026)
assumptions: Portability is assumed elected (a timely Form 706 at the first death); the code assumes this without saying so. A planner or attorney should review. Rule type: assumed. Authority: statute.

evidence.description: The combined (both-spouse) fed_exempt is indexed from plan_start to the terminal year, then federal tax = 40% of the excess
The whole base is compounded by brk_inf
A couple's default exemption is two times the per-person amount
This reference data file itself says estate-attorney review of the portability arithmetic is not documented

observed_behavior: The first decedent's ported amount is fixed at that death under 2010(c)(4), but the engine grows it to the second death. For a first death in 2030 and a second in 2050 at 2.5%, the ported half is about $16.6M in the law but about $27M in the engine.
impact: Federal estate tax can be understated by up to about 40% of the excess indexing (millions of dollars). This only matters for estates above roughly $30M, so few households are affected.
affected_workflows: Estate tax and Post-Tax Inheritance for very large estates
root_cause: One combined exemption is indexed uniformly, and nothing tracks the first-death date.
options: No credible alternative; this is a correctness defect.
recommendation: Index the survivor's own exclusion to the terminal year and freeze the DSUE at the first-death year's indexed amount. State that a timely portability election is assumed.
implementation_considerations: The first-death year is already tracked (c['first_death_yr']). The Roth optimizer's _estate_tax_for_row needs the same change.
risk_of_change: Low.
verification_method: Unit test with known first-death and second-death years, compared against a hand calculation.
verification_rationale: after_tax.py:751-753 and core.py:1467-1478 compound the whole combined fed_exempt from plan_start to the terminal year. data_io.py:963-964 defaults a couple to twice the per-person amount. roth_conversion.py:121 does the same in _estate_tax_for_row. tax_update_dashboard.csv row 12 says estate-attorney review of the portability arithmetic is not documented. Freezing DSUE at the first death (2010(c)(4)) is standard law, so the model over-indexes the ported half. The portability election is assumed and not disclosed. This only matters for very large estates (about $30M or more), so low severity is kept. The dollar example depends on the inflation and death-year assumptions.

title: S-corp income in Illinois leaves out the 1.5% Personal Property Replacement Income Tax, and a comment wrongly says it is already counted
assumptions: Applies to an Illinois-resident S corporation. The user could be absorbing it in business expenses (biz_exp), which the code cannot show. Rule type: not modeled. Authority: statute.

evidence.description: The comment says 'IL corporate surcharge on distributable income (already captured in state_tax via AGI; no separate payroll item)'
Individual state tax is the flat 4.95%. There is no entity-level replacement tax

recommendation: Add a state entity-tax rate (Illinois 1.5% for S-corps) as a dated state reference value applied to the S-corp's ordinary income. Correct the comment. Note in the help that a PTET election is not modeled.

I also found a larger problem: client_sections.py:1294 parses c['scorp_state_rate'] (state_corporate_surcharge_rate, default 0.015), and grep shows only sheets_strategy.py:165,195 reads it. title: The divorce stress scenario splits assets but keeps a married-filing-jointly two-person household

assumptions: This is a stress-test scenario, not the base plan. Rule type: simplified scenario. Authority: unverified.

title: The 401(k) model has one earner and one limit with no age-based catch-up rules
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC 402(g), 414(v) as amended by SECURE 2.0 secs. 109 and 603)
rule_year: 2025-2026 onward (super catch-up at ages 60-63 from 2025; Roth-only catch-up for prior-year FICA wages above $145k indexed, from 2026)
assumptions: The limit is entered by the user (default 32,500 = 2026 deferral plus the age-50 catch-up). Rule type: configurable, user-provided. Authority: user-provided.

evidence.description: k401_limit_yr is the user's k401_lim indexed by brk_inf. The deposit goes to owner_idx=0's 401(k) only, the cap is deferral_comp, and there is no age test
One household monthly contribution and one base-year limit (default 32500)

title: Voiding a sale linked to the transaction log says 'Use Restore to bring it back', but Restore is then refused

evidence.description: The confirm text is only 'Remove <gain> from <year> totals?'. On success it always shows 'Sale voided. Use Restore to bring it back.', whatever kind of sale it was.

For a sale whose lot_key has log_sell, voiding also voids the live transaction-log sell and rebuilds that account's holdings (materialize_managed). Unvoiding then raises ValidationError 'this lot's log sale was removed with the void; record the sale again'.

After the void, the Restore menu item for a log-linked lot is disabled with the reason 'its log sale was removed with the void: record the sale again'. So the UI knows ahead of time that this void cannot be undone, but the confirm and success text do not say so.

observed_behavior: For sales recorded through the transaction log, Void is effectively one-way: it voids the log sell, puts the shares back in their lots, and blocks Restore. The confirm dialog does not mention this. The success message promises the user can Restore.
impact: A user who voids by mistake expects a one-click undo and finds Restore disabled. They then have to re-enter the sale by hand, with the lot choice and dates, to get their realized-gain and tax-year records right again. This is the kind of 'wrong recovery promise' slip that error-prevention guidance (Nielsen heuristic 5; ISO 9241-110 error tolerance) warns against for financial records.
affected_workflows: Track & Reconcile > Investment Sales Ledger > Sales tab > lot actions > Void / Restore
Investment Holdings > Activity (transaction log) consistency after a void
root_cause: slVoid builds its confirm and success text the same way for every sale and ignores the lot_key log_sell link. The row renderer already uses that link to disable Restore.
options: No credible alternative; this is a correctness defect.
recommendation: When lot_key has log_sell, change the confirm to say this void also removes the linked Activity sale and cannot be undone with Restore (the sale must be recorded again), and drop the 'Use Restore' sentence from the success message. Move this confirm to the in-app showInAppConfirm dialog together with UX-002.
implementation_considerations: The log_sell test already exists in slLotRowHtml (lines 40-41); reuse it rather than adding a second check. Keep the message text in step with the server's ValidationError wording. Do not add a frontend test that matches source string literals (test_freeze_frontend_source_grep); use the Node vm sandbox harness.
risk_of_change: Low; this changes message text and branching only and leaves void semantics alone.
verification_method: In the Node vm sandbox, render a voided sale with a log_sell lot_key and with a manual lot_key, call slVoid, and check that the confirm and success texts differ. In the app, void a log-recorded sale on the demo plan and check that the message does not offer Restore.
verification_rationale: I opened frontend/js/dashboard_decomp_sales_ledger.js:255-261 (slVoid). The confirm text is 'Remove <gain> from <year> totals?' and the success text is always 'Sale voided. Use Restore to bring it back.', with no lot_key check. In the same file, lines 38-42 (slLotRowHtml), the Void menu item is enabled for log_sell-linked lots, and after the void Restore is disabled with the reason 'its log sale was removed with the void: record the sale again'. In src/sales_service.py:215-232 (_set_voided), voiding a sale with a log_sell link voids the live log sell and runs materialize_managed; unvoiding raises ValidationError when the sell is no longer active. So the success text promises a Restore that the UI and the server both refuse. Mitigation: the disabled Restore item does explain why, so the user is told afterward, not left confused. That keeps severity at medium, not high. The fix fits the problem and is narrow. This is not a financial-rule finding, so no jurisdiction applies.

title: Irreversible financial-record actions use bare native confirm() dialogs that understate the consequences, although an in-app confirm dialog exists

evidence.description: window.confirm('Delete <account>? Its balance is removed from the plan.') The text does not say the delete is permanent or that it removes other data.
A hard delete: it removes the account's holdings rows and its ytd_account_setup row, and clears every Monarch mapping that points at it. There is no soft-delete or undo path.
Local backups are opt-in ('Off — backups run only when enabled here'), so there is no default safety net for a mistaken delete.
Close year, Reopen year (which 'discards' frozen figures) and Mark as rollover (which changes tax treatment) all use bare global confirm().
Replacing an earlier 1099-B statement is confirmed with window.confirm, and only when window.confirm exists.

tlConfirmed returns true (consent) when window.confirm is not a function. This guards Start the log (holdings are written by the log from then on), voiding bank opening rows, and voiding a transaction.

An accessible in-app confirm already exists: it traps Tab, closes on Escape, takes a safe-default initial focus, and restores focus. The Planning Workbench uses it (planning_workbench_ui.js:287), and plan-folder import uses an in-app list confirm (dashboard_plan_folder_io.js:30).

observed_behavior: The newest record-keeping flows (cash accounts, cash-year close, rollover marking, 1099-B replace, transaction log, sale void) ask with the browser's native OK/Cancel box. The text is short, does not say whether the action can be undone, does not list side effects, and labels the buttons OK/Cancel instead of naming the action. In two helpers, a missing confirm() counts as consent.
impact: Native OK/Cancel boxes give no information scent: the user is not told what OK does, OK is the default, and habituated users click through. In this desktop app, the Delete and Void actions are permanent, or reversible only with work. The pattern also goes against the in-app dialog direction the project took (WI-018/UX-011). It cannot be styled or sized with the app's text-size control, and its focus and announcement behavior under the WebView2 shell was not established.
affected_workflows: Year-End Transition > Investment cash > Close / Reopen year, Mark as rollover
Investment Sales Ledger > 1099-B apply (replace), Void sale
Investment Holdings > Activity > Start the log, bank cleanup, Void transaction
root_cause: The record-keeping modules were written as standalone ES modules that call the global confirm() instead of the shared ctx.confirm/showInAppConfirm, and there is no project rule requiring the shared dialog for destructive actions.
options: Route every destructive record action through showInAppConfirm, with an action-named primary button ('Delete account', 'Close 2026'), a consequences line (permanent or undoable, and what else changes), and Cancel as the initial focus. Moderate effort, about 8 call sites.
Keep confirm() but rewrite each message to state permanence and side effects, and make missing-confirm mean refusal. Low effort, but it keeps the native-dialog problems.
Add server-side soft delete or undo for cash-account delete and an automatic pre-action snapshot, then use lighter confirmations. Higher effort; it touches the store layer.
recommendation: Option 1, plus changing tlConfirmed and the window.confirm && ... guards so that no dialog means no action. Consider turning on a local backup automatically before hard deletes as a follow-up.
implementation_considerations: showInAppConfirm returns a Promise. Callers such as caDelete and ciCloseYear are already async; tlConfirmed is synchronous and needs converting. The frontend line ceiling (test_frontend_size_ratchet) means the shared dialog should be reused, not a new one written. Write tests in the Node vm sandbox, not as source-text greps.
risk_of_change: Low to moderate: async conversion of a few handlers, and existing frontend tests that stub window.confirm will need updating.
verification_method: Node sandbox tests that each destructive handler calls the in-app confirm and does nothing when it is dismissed, and that a missing confirm does not proceed. Do a manual keyboard pass (Tab, Escape, initial focus on Cancel) in the desktop shell.
verification_rationale: Call sites I verified: caDelete (cash_accounts.js:59-66) uses window.confirm with 'Its balance is removed from the plan.' cash_accounts.py:98-113 (delete_account) is a hard delete that removes holdings rows and the ytd_account_setup row and clears the matching Monarch mappings, with no undo in that function. ciCloseYear, ciReopenYear and ciMarkRollover (cash_investment.js:82-100) use bare confirm(). bbApply (sales_1099b.js:176-181) is guarded by window.confirm &&. tlConfirmed (transactions_log.js:183) returns true when confirm is unavailable; a comment says this is 'by design (tests, embedded views)', which explains it but is still fail-open. local_backups.js:31-36 shows backups are off by default. showInAppConfirm and openStaticDialog (row_model.js:3312/3390, ctx.confirm at 4490-4493) exist, and planning_workbench_ui.js:287 and dashboard_plan_folder_io.js:30 use them. Caveats: some of the confirm texts do state consequences (Reopen says frozen figures are 'discarded'; Rollover explains the tax effect), so 'understates' applies most strongly to caDelete, tlVoid and the 1099-B replace. I did not open any dialog CSS, so I did not verify the claimed Cancel-first focus of showInAppConfirm. The sale-void site overlaps UX-001 but the scope is broader, so this is not a duplicate.

title: Result and error feedback for the ledger and cash panels uses freshly injected role=status paragraphs, so errors are announced politely or not at all, and the shell message slot can overwrite an unread error

evidence.description:
Both errors and successes are rendered as a new

inside the panel's re-rendered innerHTML.
Same pattern: error messages use role=status (polite), not alert.
Same pattern. The same is true for sales_entry.js:94, sales_queue.js:112, sales_tax.js:88, sales_wash.js:28 and transactions_log.js:26.
The cash/year-close panel instead uses an injected role=alert for errors. That is a second convention.
A persistent live region pair (polite and alert) exists for the ledger, but the panel messages above do not use it.
There is one header slot. Each call replaces innerHTML and switches role and aria-live on the same element, so any later info message replaces a persistent error the user has not read or dismissed.

observed_behavior: There are three feedback conventions: the shell #actionMessage, panel-local role=status or role=alert paragraphs injected with the content, and the ledger's persistent sr-only regions. Panel errors are often marked polite. Because the live-region element is created in the same update as its text, many screen-reader and browser combinations do not announce it.
impact: After pressing Apply, Void, Delete or Close year, a screen-reader user may hear nothing on success or failure, or hear a failure only politely. Sighted users see feedback in different places on different pages, which adds cognitive load and weakens consistency (WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages; Nielsen consistency and visibility of system status). An error in the shell slot can disappear when an unrelated info message replaces it.
affected_workflows: Any flow that calls showMessage after an earlier error
root_cause: Each module renders its own message markup inside its innerHTML repaint, and there is no shared announce helper that writes to a region already present in the DOM.
options: Add one shared announce(text, {error}) helper that writes to persistent polite and assertive regions in index.html (generalizing slAnnounce). Keep the visible panel text without a live role. Make showMessage keep an unread error, for example by queuing or appending, instead of replacing it.
Standardize only the visible markup (errors role=alert, successes role=status) and accept that injected regions announce unreliably.
Route all panel feedback through showMessage. This loses the message's proximity to the panel that caused it.
recommendation: Option 1. It keeps the feedback visible beside the panel and makes announcements reliable and uniform.
implementation_considerations: The project has tests named inapp_modal_accessibility and reflow-and-message-row (existence only; not run). The helper must stay inside the frontend line ceiling, so replacing the per-module message markup should be roughly line-neutral.
risk_of_change: Low to moderate; it touches many modules' message rendering, but each change is mechanical.
verification_method: Run NVDA or Narrator in the WebView2 desktop shell: trigger a success and a failure on 1099-B apply, sale void and cash-account delete, and confirm each is announced once, with errors as assertive. Add a Node sandbox test that an info showMessage after an error leaves the error reachable.
verification_rationale:
Verified: caHtml (cash_accounts.js:18), slListHtml (sales_ledger.js:89-90), bbBodyHtml (sales_1099b.js:105) and tlMsgHtml (transactions_log.js:26) render errors and successes as

inside repainted markup. The cash/year-close panel (cash_investment.js:63) uses role=alert instead. slLiveHtml and slAnnounce (sales_ledger_ui.js:140-144) exist, but slPost (sales_ledger.js:237-245) only sets slMessage and never calls slAnnounce; the only callers I found are summary changes and transactions_log.js:106. showMessage (row_model.js:195-241) overwrites innerHTML and role on the single #actionMessage slot every time it is called, so a later info call replaces a persistent error. I did not open sales_entry.js, sales_queue.js, sales_tax.js or sales_wash.js, so those extra sites are unverified.

title: The headline Build Impact cards put their definitions (5th percentile, LCV, EFTR) only in a native hover tooltip; the 'i' button does nothing when clicked or tapped

evidence.description: The help text goes only into title= and aria-label on a <button class="field-info-i">. The button has no onclick and no aria-controls="helpPanel".
The help panel opens only for elements with aria-controls="helpPanel", so these card buttons never open it.
Field-level 'i' badges include aria-controls="helpPanel" and so open the help panel. The result cards do not, which makes the two kinds of 'i' badge behave differently.

The headline cards are 'Expected After-Tax LCV', 'Worst-Case Ending Wealth' and 'Effective Future Tax Rate (EFTR)'. The visible title deliberately drops '(5th %ile)', so the only statement that 'worst case' means the 5th percentile and not the true worst case is inside the tooltip.
The 'Change / Current build' label under each headline is 9px uppercase muted text.

observed_behavior: The primary result summary uses acronyms and statistical shorthand. The definitions are visible only when a mouse hovers over a tiny 'i'. Keyboard focus does not show a native title tooltip in Chromium or WebView2, and touch cannot hover. Activating the button does nothing.
impact: Users are likely to misread the headline figures. Without the definition, 'Worst-Case Ending Wealth' reads as a floor, when 5% of simulated paths end lower. 'LCV' and 'EFTR' are unexplained jargon. Risk-communication research favors explicit, visible framing for probabilistic outcomes, not hidden glosses. Screen-reader users get the whole definition read as the button's name on every pass, which is verbose.
affected_workflows: Analyze > Build & Results > Latest Build Impact
root_cause: The card renderer predates the help-panel convention (aria-controls="helpPanel" with data-help keys), and the title was shortened for layout (#309) without moving the qualifier into visible text.
options: Wire the card 'i' into the help panel the same way field badges are (aria-controls, a help key in help_registry), and add a short visible qualifier such as '5% of paths end lower' under the Worst-Case value.
Show a one-line plain-language definition under each card title at all times, which costs vertical space.
Keep the tooltip but switch to the existing data-tip or focusable tooltip pattern that also shows on focus and tap.
recommendation: Option 1. It reuses the existing help system and puts the one qualifier that matters for risk (the percentile) in view.
implementation_considerations: help_registry entries must use glossary terms (the prose guard test, PR #267). The impact-card layout was tuned so titles do not wrap (#309 comment), so put the qualifier under the value, not in the title.
risk_of_change: Low.
verification_method: Keyboard-only: Tab to each card 'i', press Enter, and the help panel shows the definition. Visually: the Worst-Case card shows its percentile qualifier without hover. Add a Node sandbox test that impactCardHtml output carries aria-controls="helpPanel".
verification_rationale: Confirmed: impactCardHtml (build_history.js:431-433) renders a field-info-i button with only title and aria-label, with no aria-controls and no onclick. onHelpClick (help_registry.js:1097-1103) acts only on [aria-controls="helpPanel"], so the button does nothing when activated, while the field badges in dashboard.js:1617 do carry aria-controls. .impact-headline-label is 9px. Refuted in part: 'the only statement that worst case means the 5th percentile is inside the tooltip' is false whenever a before/after delta exists. buildImpactNarrativeHtml (build_history.js:565-568), rendered above the cards at line 596, visibly says 'Worst-case (5th percentile) ending wealth ...'. The qualifier is hidden only on a first build or when one side is missing. 'EFTR is unexplained jargon' is also false: the visible card title is 'Effective Future Tax Rate (EFTR)' (build_history.js:499). LCV is the only unexpanded acronym. The inert button is a real accessibility defect, but the risk-misreading impact is overstated, so I lowered severity to low.

title: Secondary tab strips use role=tab without the matching tab-panel semantics, roving focus or arrow keys; only the Sales Ledger implements the pattern

evidence.description: role=tablist with no accessible name, and role=tab buttons with onclick only: no aria-controls, no tabpanel, no roving tabindex, no arrow-key handler.
The tablist is named, but the panels below have no role=tabpanel or aria-controls link, and there is no key handling.
An unnamed tablist. The selected tab is shown with the generic 'btn good' class, so it looks different from the workspace-tab style used elsewhere.
An unnamed tablist with role=tab buttons, onclick only.

Leave as is.

Status and KPI labels at 9–10px. The impact-card title span is 10.5px.

zoomable=True, so WebView zoom is also available as a separate route to larger text.

title: Contextual help for key pages is stitched-together text from retired sub-pages, with undefined jargon and no definition of the two headline result measures
